Career Radar

A self-updating job tracker that finds the APM, internship and new grad roles I'm eligible for, and alerts me as soon as new ones are posted.

Problem

APM programs open for a few weeks a year, and many entry-level PM roles never use the word "APM." Job boards show thousands of listings, most of which I'm not eligible for. By the time I found the right roles, the best windows were already closing.

Research

I tried the existing trackers first. Each one solved part of the problem: one listed named programs, another tracked internship drops, another covered new grad roles. None filtered by my graduation date, and none told me when something new appeared.

Scope decision

I only automated sources with structured feeds, and kept sites without one as quick links instead of building scrapers that would break. Alerts fire only for product roles, which keeps them meaningful. Roles that don't state a start date get a "check" tag instead of being dropped. That way nothing good disappears without me noticing.

What I built

A Python pipeline that sweeps public job feeds every 15 minutes, filters by level, timing and field, and rebuilds a dashboard with lanes for APM programs, internships, new grad and data roles. In one snapshot it narrowed 7,686 listings to 535 eligible roles.

Design decision

The program directory and the live listings are separate on purpose. The directory is strategy: which big programs open when. The listings are action: what I can apply to today.

Roles under other titles

Early-career product roles go by many titles: new grad product manager, 2027 associate product manager, early career product manager and more. A title tagger, a set of rules that recognizes these naming patterns, catches all of them. In that same snapshot, it found 99 roles that never use the word "APM."

7,686 listings to 535 eligible 99 roles found under other titles 15-minute sweeps Desktop alerts
Read the process
  1. Why I built it

    I kept missing APM programs because their application windows are only open for a few weeks, and none of the trackers I tried could filter by my graduation date.

  2. Deciding what “eligible” means

    Before writing any code, I had to define which roles were worth showing me. Graduation date, experience level and timing turned out to matter more than the job title.

  3. Finding roles with different titles

    Plenty of early-career product roles never say “APM.” I wrote a title tagger, a set of rules that recognizes naming patterns, to flag titles such as “New Grad Product Manager” and “Early Career Product Manager.”

  4. Removing duplicates

    I pulled listings from several job feeds, which are public lists of open roles that update automatically. The same role often showed up two or three times. I matched listings by company and title and kept one copy of each, which keeps every count honest.

  5. Checking the results by hand

    The first version still let through roles that required a Master's degree. I went through the output myself, tightened the filters and checked again until none slipped through.

  6. Widening the search

    Looking only at product roles was too narrow for a real job search. I added a data and analytics track to keep my options open.

  7. Making it easier to use every day

    The first design was playful, with a lot of decoration. After using it daily, I noticed the extras made it harder to scan roles quickly, and I simplified it.

  8. What it can't do yet

    Some job sites don't offer a feed, and those stay as links I check myself. When a listing doesn't say when the job starts, I tag it to double-check rather than guessing.

What I learned: being my own user made every problem easy to spot, because I was the one who missed out when something broke.

Product Case Study · Front-End Product Build

Use It Up

A recipe matcher that shows what you can cook with what's already in your kitchen, starting with the ingredients about to expire.

Problem

People overspend on groceries and throw out food they forgot they had. I'm one of them. Nothing tells you what you can make with what you have at the moment you're deciding what to eat.

Research

Informal interviews showed the friction isn't finding recipes. It's forgetting what's already in the fridge before a shopping trip.

Scope decision

I cut barcode scanning, price tracking and grocery lists from v1 to prove the core matching loop first. Grocery lists came back once it was clear they were pure logic with no outside dependency. A live recipe API and accounts stayed out, since neither was needed to test the core idea.

What I built

A working demo with 25 recipes across 14 cuisines. It ranks recipes by how many ingredients you already have and moves the ones that use up food about to expire to the top. Anything you're missing from your planned recipes goes into one grocery list, sorted by aisle.

25 recipes, 14 cuisines Rescue-first ranking Merged grocery list Servings scaler
Read the process
  1. Why I built it

    I kept throwing out food I forgot I had. When I asked friends, most said the same thing: the hard part isn't finding recipes, it's remembering what's already in the fridge.

  2. Who it's for

    I designed it for students and people early in their careers who cook for one or two and want to waste less.

  3. What I left out

    Barcode scanning, price tracking and a live recipe database would each have needed an outside service. I left them out to test the main idea first: can the app suggest meals from what you already have?

  4. How recipes are ranked

    Recipes that use ingredients about to expire come first, then the ones that need the fewest extra items. I chose this order because, to me, wasting food is worse than one extra trip to the store.

  5. Bringing back the grocery list

    I first planned to add a grocery list later. Once I realized it didn't need any outside service, I added it: missing items from every planned recipe, combined into one list and sorted by aisle.

  6. Fixing a confusing first screen

    The first version opened with a kitchen already full of sample food, and people couldn't tell what was theirs. Now first-time visitors choose between a sample kitchen and an empty one.

  7. Small details that matter

    When you change servings, amounts round to real kitchen measurements, for example 1 1/2 cups instead of 1.4999. If a recipe photo fails to load, a drawing of the dish appears instead of an empty box.

  8. Testing with real people

    I'm running short sessions where people plan a dinner from their own fridge. I time how long it takes them to find a recipe they would cook and note where they get stuck.

What I learned: one simple rule, use the expiring food first, ended up shaping the whole product.

Product Case Study · Front-End Product Build

Closet Match

Turns your Pinterest boards into outfits, then shows which pieces you already own and which ones you're missing.

Problem

Most of us have hundreds of outfits saved on Pinterest and still stand in front of the closet with nothing to wear. Instead of pulling everything out to see what works, Closet Match helps you decide before you start digging.

Scope decision

Pinterest runs on a demo account in v1. Connecting real accounts needs a server to keep login keys private, plus an approval from Pinterest. I built the product around one small connection point that the real Pinterest link can plug into later.

What I built

A board importer that reads each pin, tags it by style, occasion and clothing pieces, and matches it against your closet. It picks up your top styles from what you pin, and every look explains why it was recommended. Missing pieces link straight to online shopping, and one tap saves them to your shopping list.

Design decision

The page starts empty instead of filling up with stock photos. Every image comes from your own boards, which makes the product feel personal from the first click.

Pinterest board import Style detection from pins Closet matching Explains every match
Read the process
  1. Why I built it

    I save outfits on Pinterest all the time, and I rarely know whether I can recreate them with what I own. That gap between loving a look and wearing it is what I wanted to close.

  2. Working with a demo account

    Connecting to real Pinterest accounts requires a server and an approval process from Pinterest. I built the app around a demo account instead, set up in a way that lets the real connection be swapped in later without rebuilding anything.

  3. Reading what's in each pin

    The app reads each pin's description and tags it by style, occasion and clothing pieces. Specific phrases take priority over general ones: “linen trousers” counts as linen trousers, not as two separate items.

  4. Skipping the style quiz

    Rather than asking people to describe their style, the app looks at what they've already saved and picks their top two styles. They can still change them.

  5. Starting with an empty page

    Before you connect, the page shows nothing. Every image comes from your own boards, which makes the results feel personal from the start.

  6. Explaining every recommendation

    Each outfit has a “Why this outfit?” button that shows which board it came from, which style it matches and how much of it you already own. I wanted people to be able to check the app's reasoning.

  7. Making missing pieces easy to shop

    Each missing piece links to an online shopping search, and a + button saves it to your shopping list. Nobody should have to look up every item on their own.

  8. What I still need to test

    I haven't measured how accurate the tagging is yet. My next step is to label a set of pins by hand and compare my labels with the app's.

What I learned: people trust recommendations more when they can see why they were made.

Selected projects

Data projects

01 · DECISION SUPPORT
Analysis complete

Athlete Burnout & Performance

Fitness is one of my biggest interests, and I wanted to know whether data could spot a bad training day before it happens. I built models on a simulated dataset to find early warning signs of a performance drop, and weighed catching more at-risk athletes against raising more false alarms.

R² = 0.656ROC-AUC = 0.84013.5K simulated records
Read the process
  1. Why I chose it

    Fitness is a big part of my life, and I know firsthand how much sleep and recovery change how a workout goes. I wanted to see whether everyday habits such as sleep, recovery and training load could warn of a performance drop before it happens.

  2. Challenges and limits

    Real athlete health data is private and hard to get. I generated a realistic practice dataset of 75 athletes over 180 days, 13,500 daily records in total, which means the results describe the simulation, not real people. Performance drops are also rare, and a model can look accurate by predicting that nothing ever goes wrong.

  3. How I handled them

    I'm upfront that the data is simulated and treated the project as practice in building and judging models. For the rare drops, I lowered the model's alert threshold, the confidence level it needs before flagging someone. That let it catch 91% of real drops, at the cost of more false alarms. For a coach, a false alarm costs a rest day, while a missed warning can cost an injury.

  4. Outcome

    The best models reached an R² of 0.656 for predicting performance scores, meaning they explain about two-thirds of the variation, and a ROC-AUC of 0.84 for spotting drops, a measure of how well they separate drops from normal days. Yesterday's performance was by far the strongest signal, followed by recovery, fatigue and sleep.

02 · DATA PRODUCT
Dashboard complete

Global Environmental Stress Index

I care about the environment, and air quality data is hard to compare from one place to the next. I combined five air-quality measures into a single index and designed an interactive dashboard that makes those comparisons easier to explore.

23K city-level records5 air-quality measures
Read the process
  1. Why I chose it

    I care about the environment, and the air we breathe is one of the most direct ways it affects people. Air quality is usually reported as several separate measurements, which makes it hard to compare places at a glance. I wanted one number that makes those comparisons easier.

  2. Challenges and limits

    Choosing how much each pollutant counts is a judgment call, and different weights would change the rankings. The data was also uneven: some countries had thousands of cities and others only one, and 427 records were missing a country.

  3. How I handled them

    I gave the most weight to the overall air quality index (40%) and fine particles, known as PM2.5 (30%), and I state clearly that the index is a comparison tool, not an official health rating. I added a city count next to every country, which shows readers when a ranking rests on a single city. I loaded the cleaned data into a SQL database, a set of tables I could query, to compare countries, cities and pollutants.

  4. Outcome

    An index covering about 23,000 cities, a Power BI dashboard for exploring it and country summaries anyone can download. The clearest pattern: in the most polluted countries, fine particles drove most of the air quality score.
